extracted.intended_audience: EPA rulewriters, FERC/Commission staff, state environmental and energy regulators, and policymakers (notice-and-comment participants)
extracted.subtask_description: Regulatory comments from NRECA on EPA's Proposed Carbon Pollution Emission Guidelines (the CPP/Section 111(d) proposal), arguing legal, technical, timing, and reliability criteria that EPA and states must respect in any final rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit BSER to within‑the‑fence improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: BSER must be limited to those emissions improvements that can be achieved within the fence line of each designated source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA has no statutory authority to define the “best system of emission reduction” in a way that goes beyond technological or operational improvements that can be made at an individual source; outside‑the‑fence measures (e.g., re‑dispatch, system‑level redispatch, demand reductions) are impermissible and cannot serve as the basis for binding state targets.

rubrics_metrics.name: States must set standards and apply them unit‑by‑unit with source‑specific considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: States establish their own standards of performance and then apply those standards on a unit‑by‑unit basis after considering source‑specific factors such as the remaining useful life of each source, the reasonableness of the associated costs, physical impossibility, and other factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA may determine what systems have been adequately demonstrated (BSER), but it cannot set fixed, binding statewide limits that usurp the statutory state role; states must be allowed to consider remaining useful life, reasonableness of costs, and physical limitations when assigning unit‑specific limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibit double regulation of source categories already regulated under Section 112
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 111(d) (as amended) prohibits regulating existing source categories under 111(d) if they are already regulated under Section 112 (e.g., coal‑fired EGUs regulated by MATS).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because coal plants came under Section 112 regulation in 2012 (MATS), EPA cannot lawfully regulate them under Section 111(d); the House amendment controls and double‑regulation is barred.

rubrics_metrics.name: 111(d) prerequisite: valid NSPS under Section 111(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA may not promulgate an existing source standard under Section 111(d) without first adopting a valid new source performance standard (NSPS) under Section 111(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the proposed 111(b) NSPS or the modified/reconstructed source standard is invalid, the statutory predicate for an 111(d) rule is not satisfied and the 111(d) rule cannot be finalized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide substantially longer SIP development timelines (5/7 years plus extension)
rubrics_metrics.description: States should be given at least five years to develop a SIP if acting alone and seven years if part of a multi‑State group, with an additional up to three years available upon demonstration of reasonable progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA’s proposed 1‑3 year submission deadlines are unrealistically short given the rule’s complexity; longer timelines are necessary to allow for legal, regulatory, engineering, transmission, and market changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow compliance deadlines based on remaining useful life; set earliest final compliance date no earlier than 2035
rubrics_metrics.description: States should be allowed to adopt compliance deadlines based on the remaining useful lives of each designated facility, and EPA should permit extension of statewide compliance dates at least to 2035 where necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unit‑specific final compliance dates should be based on evidence (e.g., loan documents) of remaining useful life to avoid premature retirements, stranded investments, and to ensure staged build‑out of needed infrastructure and labor capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandon interim emission reduction targets
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must abandon the interim targets it has proposed because they will be impossible for most, if not all, States to meet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interim targets undermine state flexibility and reliability planning and should be removed from any final rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt a dynamic reliability safety valve
rubrics_metrics.description: A dynamic reliability safety valve must be provided that allows each state’s goal to change as system conditions change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States should be able to adjust goals in response to events such as unexpected nuclear plant closures, gas delivery constraints, transmission delays, renewable delivery limitations, economic growth, or other reliability threats to avoid forcing choices between compliance and leaving customers without reliable power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust lb./MWh reduction goals for cooperatives' practical constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: If EPA insists on binding statewide emission reduction goals, the lb./MWh reduction goals must be adjusted upward to reflect the limited ability of rural electric cooperatives and similarly situated utilities to comply with BSER.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many cooperatives have limited portfolios, rely heavily on coal, face financing/lessor constraints, have limited opportunities for heat‑rate improvements or demand‑side reductions, and thus cannot meet EPA’s optimistic assumptions without disproportionate burdens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assume static grid conditions from baseline to 2030
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA’s assumption of fairly static conditions on the electric grid between the 2012 baseline and 2030 is unrealistic and cannot form the basis for fixed state targets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grid conditions are dynamic (generation retirements/additions, transmission constraints, fuel markets, technology changes) and targets or compliance mechanisms must allow for changing conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Building Blocks must be demonstrably achievable and record‑based
rubrics_metrics.description: Each of EPA’s Building Blocks (heat‑rate improvements; re‑dispatch to NGCC; increased nuclear/renewables; end‑use energy efficiency) must be demonstrably achievable and supported by reliable record evidence before being used to set targets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NRECA identifies specific flaws: HRI studies do not support EPA’s assumptions; NGCC 70% capacity factor presumption is unsupported; transmission and renewable buildout assumptions are unsupported; inclusion of end‑use efficiency exceeds authority of EPA/state agencies; if any building block is invalid the BSER construct fails.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPA methods should be guidance, not mandatory requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA’s proposed methods for translating BSER and setting state targets can only be applied as guidance to the States and not as binding requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the statute reserves primary authority to the States to set performance standards and account for unit‑specific factors, EPA’s methodologies can inform but not compel state plans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect fuel diversity and near‑term baseload coal capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule must protect a diverse fuel mix and maintain existing coal plant capacity as a baseload fuel, particularly in the near term, because fuel diversity supports affordability, reliability, and national security.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unnecessary early retirements of coal units threaten reliability (e.g., during extreme weather events), increase exposure to gas delivery problems and price volatility, and disproportionately impact rural consumers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for cumulative regulatory impacts on rates and 'just and reasonable' standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulators must consider the cumulative impact of EPA’s regulations (including Section 111(d)) on the entire resource portfolio to ensure outcomes are just, reasonable, and affordable for consumers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A dynamic reliability safety valve and recognition of cumulative costs are necessary to balance environmental benefits against reliability and affordability obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve state flexibility to implement compliance measures
rubrics_metrics.description: The Clean Air Act requires that States be given maximum flexibility in determining how to achieve compliance with emission standards they develop.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA must not supplant state choices with uniform mandates; flexibility includes timing, selection of measures, and accounting for local/regional constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: If any Building Block is invalid, strike EPA’s BSER definition
rubrics_metrics.description: If any one of EPA’s Building Blocks (1–4) is legally or technically invalid, the entire BSER as defined by EPA must be stricken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because EPA defines BSER as the combination of building blocks, the invalidity of a component undermines the entire BSER determination and thus the foundation for state targets.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPA must identify the nature and scope of Federal Implementation Plans (FIPs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a State fails to submit a satisfactory plan, EPA should identify in the rulemaking both the nature and the scope of the federal implementation plans it would prescribe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stakeholders need clarity on potential federal backstop measures so states and regulated entities can plan; vague threats of FIPs are inadequate for meaningful comment or planning.
